title: A high-performance quantum pulse gate in thin-film lithium niobate
authors: Silia Babel, Alejandra Alarcón, Laura Serino, Christian Golla, Laura Bollmers, Sebastian Lengeling, Jiayu Yang, Bernhard Reineke, Christof Eigner, Benjamin Brecht, Marko Lončar, Laura Padberg, Christine Silberhorn
abstract: In this work, we demonstrate a quantum pulse gate (QPG) in thin-film lithium niobate. QPGs enable the selective manipulation and detection of temporal modes of quantum light and form the basis of numerous applications in photonic quantum technologies. To date, their widespread adaption is held back by two main limitations: restricted wavelength and polarization combinations of the involved fields and low normalized conversion efficiencies. We overcome these limitations through developing a QPG in thin-film lithium niobate. We design a waveguide geometry that provides the required dispersion properties for a highly efficient type-0 sum-frequency generation.We verify our design through mapping of the phase matching intensity, and demonstrate high-quality QPG operation by measuring a temporal-mode selectivity of (96.8$\pm$1.7)% on par with existing QPGs. Thanks to the strong confinement in thin-film lithium niobate, we succeed in demonstrating an internal conversion efficiency of (89.6$\pm$0.1)% for a pump power of only 20mW in front of our sample. This yields a lower-bound estimate for the normalized conversion efficiency of (1810$\pm$10)$\mathrm{W}^{-1}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$, three orders of magnitude higher than in previous QPGs. Our results establish thin-film lithium niobate as ideal platform for high-performance QPGs and are a major step towards practical QPGs for photonic quantum technologies.
summary: The paper reports on the successful demonstration of a high-performance Quantum Pulse Gate using thin-film lithium niobate. By engineering the waveguide geometry, they overcame previous limitations in efficiency and spectral flexibility. The resulting device shows state-of-the-art performance, establishing TFLN as an ideal platform for practical photonic quantum technologies.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a high-performance Quantum Pulse Gate (QPG) for photonic quantum technologies, overcoming limitations in efficiency and operational flexibility.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a QPG in thin-film lithium niobate with an average temporal-mode selectivity of $(96.8 \pm 1.7)\%$ and achieved a normalized conversion efficiency estimate three orders of magnitude higher than previous devices.
method: The work combines numerical simulations (using Lumerical) to design the waveguide geometry for optimal phase matching, followed by experimental measurements using single-photon detectors to characterize selectivity and conversion efficiency.
model_or_system: The physical platform is thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN), which enables a highly efficient type-0 Sum-Frequency Generation (SFG) process. The QPG relies on engineering waveguide dispersion to achieve group-velocity matching between input and pump fields.
key_observables: Temporal-mode selectivity ($ ar{S}$), internal conversion efficiency ($\eta$), and normalized conversion efficiency ($\eta_{	ext{norm}}$).
important_parameters: High nonlinearity ($d_{33} = 27 	ext{ pm/V}$ in TFLN), specific waveguide dimensions ($w=1 \mu	ext{m}, h=500 	ext{ nm}$), and operating wavelengths ($\lambda_{	ext{in}} = 1540 	ext{ nm}$, $\lambda_p = 860 	ext{ nm}$).
main_assumptions: The reported normalized conversion efficiency is a conservative lower bound due to uncorrected coupling estimates; the analysis assumes successful dispersion engineering compensates for material limitations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the simulation setup, phase matching intensity maps showing optimal geometry selection, and plots comparing measured internal conversion efficiency versus pump power against theoretical fits.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the need for high-performance QPGs to detailing the TFLN platform's advantages. It covers design simulations (geometry optimization), experimental setup description, measurement of selectivity, and finally, quantitative characterization of the record-breaking conversion efficiency.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware realization in quantum optics by demonstrating a scalable, high-efficiency component (QPG) crucial for building integrated photonic quantum circuits, which is highly relevant to quantum information processing architectures.

Simulation for finding a suitable waveguide geometry for a TFLN QPG. a) Waveguide geometry in TFLN with the important parameters. b) The heat map shows the phase matching angle 𝜙PM for different top widths 𝑤and etching depths ℎ. From these simulations we choose the geometry marked with the red rectangle. c) Group velocity as function of the wavelength for the chosen geometry. We mark the output, pump and input signal. The horizontal line shows that this geometry yields group velocity matching between input signal and pump. d) Simulated phase matching intensity |Φ(𝜆in, 𝜆out)|2. Due to group velocity matching the phase matching is oriented horizontally.

Fig. 2. Sketch of the experimental setup for benchmarking the TFLN QPG. The input signal and pump TMs are shaped using a commercial and a home-built waveshaper, respectively. Both fields are coupled to the sample and the generated green output light is measured with a single-photon sensitive spectrometer while the transmitted input signal photons are counted with superconducting nanowire single photon detectors. BS: beam splitter, 𝜆

Fig. 3. Map of the phase matching intensity |Φ(𝜆in, 𝜆out)|2. The angle of the phase matching function evaluates to 𝜙PM = (−3.0 ± 0.3)◦, thus verifying operation close to perfect group velocity matching. The inset shows a cut through the phase matching intensity at 𝜆in = 1550 nm. The two prominent side lobes to the left of the main peak are likely caused by fabrication imperfections and will be spectrally filtered during further measurements.

Fig. 4. Temporal-mode selectivity plots for a) high and b) low input signal photon numbers. The numbers are the percentage of converted counts of a specific input signal TM for different pump TMs. The average temporal-mode selectivity for high photon numbers of around 3 · 104 per pulse is (96.8 ± 1.7)%, while it slightly reduces to (91.7±3.1)% for an average photon number of one per pulse, likely due to measurement noise.

Figure 4 a) shows the results for pump and input powers of 2.0 mW and 0.3 µW (corresponding to around 3 · 104 photons per input pulse) in front of the waveguide, respectively.
